entries.title: White Sox still want the division title, but earning a playoff berth 'would be everything'
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> have grander ambitions than the third wild card spot, or even the American League Central title.</p><p>“If we get to do what we want to do, we’re going to be playing in the ALDS, CS and hopefully the World Series,” said Grant Taylor.</p><p>But assistant general manager Jin Wong was the White Sox executive accompanying the team for their road series in Kansas City on Tuesday. After a victory and a Rangers loss to the Mets lowered the White Sox' magic number for clinching a wild card berth to two entering Wednesday, Chris Getz and Josh Barfield flew into town to join him.</p><p>It doesn’t appear Getz is in town to deliver a postgame message to the team about the importance of staying focused on catching the Cleveland Guardians. The franchise’s first playoff appearance in five years is something to celebrate.</p><p>“It would be everything,” starter Davis Martin said of the Sox clinching a playoff spot. “We've been wrapped up in the division [race], and that's still something that's been our goal since the beginning. But from a standpoint of where we've been the last three years, just to be a part of something like that and to turn around and be the spark plug to something that maybe continues on for five, six, seven, eight years, it's just exciting.”</p><p>Martin is the longest-tenured player on the White Sox, which only means he’s been around since 2022, but plenty of suffering has been packed into that window of time. He can remember being asked “how do you sleep at night” in interviews in 2024, as if playing for a bad baseball team was a black mark on his life. Even friends and family asked if he’d rather just be traded, just to get away.</p><p>“I told all of them: my goal would be to be a part of the team that turns it around,” Martin told the Sun-Times. “To be in the situation we are now, which felt like a pipe dream two years ago, and now it’s sitting there looking at you in the face. It's incredible.”</p><p>There’s historical precedent for how incredible it is for the White Sox to make the playoffs at all. No team in MLB history has reached the postseason after three-consecutive 100-loss seasons, and the expanded playoff field can only do so much to blunt that accomplishment. But Sox players — when they’re not quoting their dire preseason projections — more sharply note the difference in how it <i>feels</i> to be part of this team, compared to just two years prior.</p><p>“In the beginning of the year, nobody really believed in us and what we are doing and now look at us,” said All-Star third baseman Miguel Vargas. “If we do it, it’s going to mean a lot for us. I think it’s a special moment.”</p><p>Manager Will Venable has been cherishing moments in places like Kauffman Stadium in Kansas City and Busch Stadium in St. Louis that lack prominent out-of-town scoreboards to distract his players, and himself. But on nights like Wednesday, where the result of Rangers-Mets could dictate whether it’s possible for the Sox to clinch a historic playoff berth, and the result of Guardians-Red Sox could mean there’s a chance to pull ahead in the AL Central, it’s hard not to get curious.</p><p>"It's been a challenge the last couple of weeks, honestly,” Venable said. “It's part of this. It's the position that we've earned, that we're in.”</p><p>It will also say a lot about what the Sox are doing in the visitor’s locker room after the game. Teams like the Dodgers or Yankees might celebrate a Wild Card spot with a polite champagne toast and a short speech about larger goals. A team like the White Sox, with their shared history, will go a different route.</p><p>“It’s not really our speed,” Martin said of a polite toast. “We kind of do everything full-go. I don’t expect it to be casual.”</p>

entries.title: Idaho authorities present new lead on Tylenol murders tied to recently identified man
entries.summary: <p>A recently identified Idaho man who died in 1982 — known as the “Unknown Wanderer” — could have ties to the four-decade-old Tylenol murders case, according to law enforcement agencies in Idaho.</p><p>Dr. Matthew Francis Betkouski died of cyanide poisoning in the pews of a Boise church in 1982, with $1,900 cash and recently dyed hair, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://adacounty.id.gov/sheriff/news/acso-solves-decades-old-unknown-wanderer-cold-case/" target="_blank" >Ada County sheriff’s office</a>.</p><p>The agency, which had been searching for the man's identity for decades, is being careful not to officially name Betkouski as a suspect in the murders even though Sheriff Matt Clifford announced evidence is going to be presented as part of an upcoming Roku documentary titled “Unmasking the Tylenol Killer” set to premiere Oct. 9.</p><p>The Ada County sheriff’s office is also sharing relevant evidence with Chicago police that may be connected to the murders.</p><p>“More information does exist in this case that we won’t be releasing today,” said Tim Cooper, a detective with the Ada County sheriff's office. “Our goal today is to generate leads in this case or others.”</p><p>Seven Chicago-area people died in September 1982 after ingesting cyanide-laced Tylenol. Johnson & Johnson recalled every form of the over-the-counter drug and created more tamper-proof pills and packaging as law enforcement searched for the culprit.</p><p>Chicago police Wednesday confirmed it had been in contact with the Ada County authorities regarding the case to “determine whether there is a connection to the Tylenol murders investigation, which remains an open cold case.”</p><p>James Lewis, a longtime leading suspect, was sentenced to 10 years in prison for extortion nearly a year later for demanding $1 million from Johnson & Johnson “<a class="Link" entries.title: Alex Bregman ‘felt like I got hit by a baseball bat to the face,’ working to make quick return to Cubs
entries.summary: <p>Trust me, you don’t want to be <b>Alex Bregman</b> right now.</p><p>“I felt like I got hit by a baseball bat to the face, pretty much,” the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ third baseman said Wednesday, three days after he took a foul ball to the face while standing on deck during a game in Cincinnati.</p><p>Bregman and the Cubs have said they’ve received relative <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/22/cubs-alex-bregman-not-on-injured-list-regular-season-playoffs" >“great news” since</a>, in terms of a potential return, one that could come as soon as this weekend.</p><p>But while that would be a boost to the Cubs’ chances as they approach the most meaningful games of their season, he’s dealing with some significant aftereffects, with multiple facial fractures.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/T7ZbU-xz3UU?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Alex Bregman on taking a baseball to the face"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>“The pain’s been fine,” Bregman said. “I guess I fractured something right by the nerve in my face, so the whole left side of my face has been a little bit numb. As soon as the swelling goes down, I’m sure I’ll feel the breaks a little bit more.</p><p>“But all in all, I’m super lucky that it hit where it hit. A lot of gratitude, because if it was a few centimeters higher, it could have been detrimental.”</p><p>And here’s some more body horror:</p><p>“There’s a lot of fluid in my face,” Bregman said. “If I move, the fluid moves. If I’m bouncing up and down, my face feels like it’s bouncing up and down.”</p><p>All that is to illustrate what Bregman’s dealing with. But being the lauded hard-worker he is, it’s little surprise that he’s champing at the bit to get back in the lineup.</p><p>“[Tuesday] was brutal. I wanted to play,” he said. “I hope [to play this weekend]. We’ll see. One step at a time. I don’t know. I’m going to try to get in there [Wednesday].”</p><p>That last line was a joke, in case you were wondering. Bregman still has a lot to test out to see how he feels and how realistic such a quick comeback is.</p><p>“He’s doing well. But we’ve got to take some steps here,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “I’m excited how he feels, and he’s excited. But he still needs to feel some things. He hasn’t run around yet, and he’s got to do that. He’s got to know what it feels like.</p><p>“We’ve got to be careful, and we’ve got to go through the proper steps.”</p><h3><b>Bummer of a bunt</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Utility man <b>Matt Shaw</b> entered Wednesday with a .176 batting average in his last 18 games.</p><p>He got a chance to help produce a run in extra innings Tuesday, but he popped up a bunt attempt with two men on and nobody out in the 10th inning of an eventual 8-2 loss.</p><p>It’s a relative nit to pick from a game in which the Cubs went 1-for-18 with runners in scoring position, but with a lot on the line in the season’s final week, it could be among the moments that loom large.</p><p>“These are the moments you prepare for,” Shaw said. “I know that I’m going to have a situation again where I’m going to have to put a bunt down. We all know what the stakes are. All we can do is keep preparing for these moments.</p><p>“An experience like this is going to help the next time I’m in that situation, and that’s all you can walk away with.”</p><h3><b>Palencia back?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Since allowing seven runs in his first five outings after a lengthy IL stint, righty reliever <b>Daniel Palencia</b> hasn’t allowed an earned run in seven straight appearances, helpful as the Cubs look for their bullpen to stabilize before the postseason begins.</p>

entries.title: Struggling at the end of a great year, White Sox reliever Sean Newcomb feels he's gotten too predictable
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. — The <b>Sean Newcomb </b>fastball that Tigers infielder <b>Hao-Yu Lee</b> hit for a game-tying home run last Friday against the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> sizzled in at 96.7 mph.</p><p>That was frustrating, but also answered a question for a reliever who has already logged 88 innings on the year.</p><p>“It’s not a stuff thing,” Newcomb told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Instead, Newcomb attributes a 10.80 ERA in September to becoming too predictable. His four-seam fastball has been one of the best pitches in the sport, but Lee homered on the fifth four-seamer of that at-bat.</p><p>Newcomb has struggled to land his slurve to get ahead in counts too, but feels this stretch resembles an earlier point of the season when he was getting beat on too many fastballs.</p><p>“The frustrating part is me not realizing it right away,” Newcomb said. “Pushing through it instead of taking a step back, looking at the big picture.”</p><h3><b>Opening jitters</b></h3><p>Before tossing two scoreless innings on Wednesday, Newcomb’s only scoreless appearance in September was also the only scoreless outing for a White Sox “opener” in their last four usages, as <b>Bryan Hudson</b> was touched up for four runs (three earned) on Wednesday night before giving way to <b>Erick Fedde</b>.</p><p>The Sox have prioritized handedness matchups in the first inning all season, with Wednesday being their MLB-leading 31st use of an opener, and show no signs of backing down.</p><p>“It's an approach that we feel strongly about, specifically with Fedde,” said manager Will Venable. “Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. But it's something we feel strongly gave us the best chance today.”</p>

entries.title: Kevin Gausman bangs up shoulder, Cubs lose another to Marlins: ‘The baseball gods are going to test you’
entries.summary: <p>If back-to-back losses with a chance to clinch a playoff spot weren’t frustrating enough for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>, here’s a new potential complication at the very end of the regular season.</p><p>Kevin Gausman – the righty pitcher who headlined <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >Jed Hoyer’s trade-deadline haul</a> and figured to be a candidate to log significant playoff innings after helping the Blue Jays to the World Series last season – banged his left shoulder while making a diving play at third base in the sixth inning of Wednesday’s 3-2 loss to the Marlins. He exited the game with the trainer.</p><p>Is it a big deal? Something that could possibly impact his effectiveness or availability come the start of the postseason, just a few days away?</p><p>The best Gausman and the Cubs had Wednesday night after the game was that they’ll wait and see.</p><p>“I dislocated this shoulder in high school, a long time ago. I didn’t necessarily do the exact same thing, but I just kind of banged it good,” Gausman said. “I felt fine until I stood up to check the other runner, and it felt like the left shoulder was pretty weak at that point.</p><p>“It still feels pretty weak, but we’ll see how it feels tomorrow and get some treatment. Hopefully, it’s just a couple-day thing.</p><p>“I hope I wake up and feel great tomorrow. But you never know. I’ll get on some medicine and get some treatment, try to get in front of it tonight. It’s just a wait-and-see type thing.”</p><p>Though they hope it’s nothing serious, the Cubs can’t afford another pitching headache at the moment, not with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-red-sox-friday-doubleheader-boston-weather-forecast-nl-wild-card-standings-mlb-playoffs-postseason" >nasty weather in Boston jumbling up their final series</a> of the regular season against the Red Sox this weekend. Those games – two of which will now be played in a Friday doubleheader – will be meaningful, with the NL wild-card standings bunched up and home-field advantage in the opening-round, best-of-three series up for grabs.</p><p>It’ll be challenging enough for the Cubs to get through the weekend, with its scheduling chaos, and set up their playoff rotation the way they want to. Anything limiting Gausman would make matters that much more complicated.</p><p>But the Cubs have to get to the playoffs first, still not something that seems unlikely; they’d have to lose all of their final four games, with the Diamondbacks winning their last four, to completely collapse and miss the postseason altogether.</p><p>That has been what’s happened in the first two games of the regular season’s final week, though, with the Cubs dropping each of the first two contests in a home series with the sub-.500 Marlins, an opponent that seemingly offered an opportunity to punch their playoff ticket, certainly when compared to this weekend’s foe, the playoff-bound Red Sox.</p><p>But the offense has gone as cold as the Wrigley Field conditions at a bad time, with the Cubs following up Tuesday’s 1-for-18 showing with runners in scoring position by going 1-for-8 in such situations Wednesday, Dansby Swanson’s broken-bat two-run single only briefly getting the Cubs out of trailing position before a video-reviewed double-play ball was flipped into an RBI ground out that gave the Marlins the lead for good in the next inning.</p><p>“It always seems like the baseball gods are going to test you, and it always seems to come at a time when you don’t want it to,” Gausman said. “But those are the things that are going to happen at this time of the year. It’s how you bounce back when those things do happen, when you get punched in the face.</p><p>“This group, since I’ve been here, has been resilient, and they were a lot before I was here. You can bank on those guys being ready to go.”</p>

entries.title: Girl sexually assaulted on way to school in Brainerd
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for a teen boy carrying a clear bookbag who sexually assaulted a girl walking to her elementary school in Brainerd on the Far South Side Wednesday morning. </p><p>She was walking to Fort Dearborn Elementary around 7:50 a.m. Wednesday in the 1300 block of West 91st Street when the boy then forced her into an alley and sexually assaulted her, Chicago police said.</p><p>The teen was described as 13 to 14 years old with dreadlocks with orange tips, wearing a black jacket or black long sleeve shirt with white writing, gray pants and carrying a clear school bookbag, police said.</p><p>Anyone with information is encouraged to contact detectives at 312-492-3810.<br></p>

Trump, once again, retaliates against journalists who offend him
entries.summary: <p>"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish," President Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117308890736529824" target="_blank" >declared</a> Monday. "It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS."</p><p>Trump was attempting to rebut the criticism provoked by his <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117293599348325006" target="_blank" >announcement</a> Friday that he was "banning" CNN, MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) and Politico "from the White House," with "other Fake News Media Outlets to follow." But his defense merely confirmed his long-standing contempt for the freedom he claims to cherish.</p><p>If you don't cover me the way I like, Trump says, I will not let you cover me at all. </p><p>"It's difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment," <a class="Link" href="https://freedom.press/issues/fpf-comments-on-trumps-media-ban-announcement/" target="_blank" >said</a> Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4f0000" name="module-4f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>The targeted news outlets responded with a First Amendment <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.296754/gov.uscourts.dcd.296754.1.0_1.pdf" target="_blank" >lawsuit</a> that was assigned to U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee who figured in an earlier legal skirmish between the president and the press. During his first term, Trump <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2018/11/16/federal-judge-rules-trump-white-house/" target="_blank" >revoked</a> CNN reporter Jim Acosta's White House press pass, later <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/judge-hands-cnn-victory-in-its-bid-to-restore-jim-acostas-white-house-press-pass/2018/11/16/8bedd08a-e920-11e8-a939-9469f1166f9d_story.html" target="_blank" >explaining</a> that Acosta was not treating him with the "respect" he deserved.</p><p>In response to a CNN <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.201611/gov.uscourts.dcd.201611.1.0_1.pdf" target="_blank" >lawsuit</a>, Kelly issued a temporary restraining order <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/judge-hands-cnn-victory-in-its-bid-to-restore-jim-acostas-white-house-press-pass/2018/11/16/8bedd08a-e920-11e8-a939-9469f1166f9d_story.html" target="_blank" >blocking</a> Acosta's banishment on <a class="Link" href="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/99/CNN_v._Trump_transcript_2018-11-16.pdf" target="_blank" >due process grounds</a>. The White House avoided a full airing of CNN's First Amendment claims by backing down. After it restored Acosta's press pass, CNN <a class="Link" href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/8169022/cable-news-network-inc-v-trump/" target="_blank" >agreed</a> to drop the lawsuit.</p><p>Shortly after beginning his second term, Trump <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/02/12/trump-bans-ap-from-oval-office-for-not-saying-gulf-of-america/" target="_blank" >barred</a> Associated Press reporters from the Oval Office, Air Force One and White House briefings because the organization had refused to start calling the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf America, the name the president <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/restoring-names-that-honor-american-greatness/" target="_blank" >prefers</a>. Two months later, another Trump-appointed judge, Trevor N. McFadden, <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.277682/gov.uscourts.dcd.277682.46.0.pdf" target="_blank" >issued</a> a preliminary injunction blocking enforcement of the AP ban, saying the organization was likely to succeed in its claims that the White House had engaged in unconstitutional retaliation and viewpoint discrimination.</p><p>The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit partially <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cadc.41932/gov.uscourts.cadc.41932.01208746547.0_1.pdf" target="_blank" >stayed</a> McFadden's order in June 2025, drawing a distinction between "limited spaces" such as the Oval Office and "events open to all credentialed White House journalists," such as East Room press conferences. The appeals court heard oral argument in the <a class="Link" href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/69869862/associated-press-v-taylor-budowich/" target="_blank" >case</a> last November but has not issued a decision yet.</p><p>The bans that Trump announced last week go at least as far as his retaliation against the AP. And it was clear from his remarks that he would like to go even further.</p><p>"Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States," Trump <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117293599348325006" target="_blank" >wrote</a> on Truth Social. "I don't think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day," he <a class="Link" href="https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-remarks-healthcare-drug-prices-oval-office-september-18-2026/" target="_blank" >told</a> reporters. "There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories."</p><p>That attitude is consistent with Trump's <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/01/18/how-the-fcc-became-the-speech-police/" target="_blank" >oft-repeated threats</a> to revoke broadcast licenses in response to news coverage he views as unfair. Brendan Carr, the Trump-appointed chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, has <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/08/26/brendan-carrs-vendetta-against-abc-conflates-the-public-interest-with-trumps-personal-grievances/" target="_blank" >taken steps</a> toward delivering on those threats, based on the <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/22/trumps-threats-to-yank-broadcast-licenses-are-part-of-a-speech-chilling-intimidation-campaign/" target="_blank" >premise</a> that broadcasters are legally obligated to please the president.</p><p>Trump's banishment of disfavored news organizations extends that assault to other media. Unlike broadcasters, cable outlets and newspapers are not subject to the "public interest" obligation that Trump and Carr conflate with a duty to avoid offending the president.</p><p>Trump also has tried to intimidate news organizations with lawsuits preposterously claiming that journalism he does not like qualifies as <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2025/11/18/court-rejects-trump-big-lie-defamation-lawsuit-00656548" target="_blank" >defamation</a> or <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/04/01/trumps-war-on-the-press/" target="_blank" >consumer fraud</a>. According to Trump, even <a class="Link" href="https://www.americanprogress.org/article/the-trump-administrations-1-7-billion-national-guard-deployments-fail-to-reduce-urban-crime/" target="_blank" >questioning</a> the effectiveness of his National Guard deployment in the District of Columbia can <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/08/31/a-liberal-think-tank-and-an-air-force-major-are-trumps-latest-targets-for-speech-policing/" target="_blank" >expose you</a> to a $5 billion defamation lawsuit.</p><p>Trump said he was "proud to announce" the sanctions against CNN, MS NOW and Politico. He should instead be embarrassed to indulge in such vendettas, which expose not only his thin-skinned pettiness but also his disregard for the First Amendment rights he <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/restoring-freedom-of-speech-and-ending-federal-censorship/" target="_blank" >pretends</a> to defend.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cc0000" name="module-cc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Press will prevail against Trump's attacks
entries.summary: <p>“To offend a strong man, tell him a lie. To offend a weak man, tell him the truth.”</p><p>That quote, often attributed to Marcus Aurelius, one of the great Stoics, perfectly encapsulates the very troubling and sad moment we’re in, and the very troubling and sad president we’re dealing with.</p><p>For all his bluster, Donald Trump is inarguably weak and small. His ego is easily bruised; his feelings are easily hurt. He’s been this way for a long time, and as Americans living in the Trump era, we’ve all come to see how deeply insecure, petty and vengeful he can be.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-260000" name="module-260000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>His late-night social media rants lashing out at enemies both real and imagined; his impetuous and impolitic attacks on longtime allies who don’t roll over for him; his reckless primarying of his own party members who dare break from him, even if momentarily.</p><p>Hell, you could even say his very presidency is the result of an otherwise harmless roast by former President Barack Obama at the 2011 White House Correspondents Dinner that he took too personally.</p><p>But when things are going particularly badly for him, his skin is at its paper thinnest, and it shows.</p><p>Last week, Trump announced on social media that he was banning three news outlets — MS NOW, Politico and CNN, where I work — from covering the White House. He hasn’t said why those particular outlets were targeted, giving the impression that this might not have been all that well thought out. Imagine that.</p><p>It does coincide, however, with Trump’s steadily sinking approval numbers, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.newsweek.com/donald-trump-approval-rating-hits-all-time-low-12467727" target="_blank" >just this week</a> hit an abysmal record low, falling below 30% according to one poll.</p><p>Believe it or not, focusing on ballrooms and buildings, invading Greenland and Canada, suing political enemies and chasing crypto deals while we’re in an ill-advised war and most Americans are stretching to afford basic necessities, have not endeared him to voters.</p><p>It’s almost as if ignoring his key promises to voters — to lower inflation, to lower the cost of goods, to never get us into another war — has turned them off.</p><p>So, stuck in a bed of his own making with nowhere to go, he’s lashing out, this time at the press, simply for covering the bad decisions he’s made and their impact on voters.</p><p>But trying to punish or sideline the press will not change the fact that he and Republicans are in deep trouble. All it does is make him look brittle, desperate and weak.</p><p>It’s also a deeply disingenuous effort. Trump has <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117308890736529824" target="_blank" >justified</a> his tantrum by saying the press is both “purposeful” and “fully coordinated” in reporting “fiction and lies.”</p><p>There’s a legal mechanism for the thing he’s talking about, and tellingly, he isn’t using it. Because, if true, what he’s describing is the textbook definition of actual malice, the legal bar used for defamation cases.</p><p>But he’s not suing the press, because this isn’t about the law, but rather his feelings. And it’s simply not our job to protect his feelings, or only publish news that makes him feel good. We’re not his parents or his kindergarten teachers.</p><p>He can throw all the fits he wants, and there’s no doubt his continual attacks on the press have had a chilling effect, but I know one thing: Ultimately, the press will win this battle.</p><p>He may wish he were president of Russia or North Korea, where the free press doesn’t exist and state media tells only positive stories about Dear Leader, but here in America, the press is protected. Here, Americans want to live in a democracy, not a dictatorship. And here, we expect our political leaders to be able to take a metaphorical punch. Especially if the “punch” in question is simply the truth.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6d0000" name="module-6d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Dear Abby: Feels like I have no choice but to let irresponsible daughter move in
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a widow who lost my husband 15 years ago. When my husband died, we had a daughter and one grandson. My daughter, a single mom, later had another son.</p><p>I have my own business and have worked hard these many years to help support my daughter, who is financially irresponsible. She has been evicted four times in the past 10 years, had two cars repossessed and can't seem to keep a job for even a year. I am at my wits' end. I need to stop helping her financially because it's affecting my financial and mental health. She doesn't have a job and can't get her own place, so I feel I have no choice but to let her move in with me. I want to put a limit on how long she can stay. What should I do? — <i>SUBJUGATED IN TEXAS</i></p><p><b>DEAR SUBJUGATED:</b> Do not allow your daughter to move in with you. If she does, you will never get rid of her. Give her a certain amount of money for shelter and make it plain that she must use it to find a place to live (if only temporarily). Because it's the last handout she'll receive, she must get a job to support herself and her children. Then let her live the life she has chosen for herself. If you don't, you will be your dysfunctional daughter's prisoner until the day you die.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Throughout my professional career, I was a quality assurance engineer with the task of analysis and corrective actions. If something broke or an error was made (for example, a worker's hand getting caught in a machine), I'd try to identify a fix so it wouldn't happen again. I am now retired and still tend to approach things with the same attitude.</p><p>I often get frustrated when someone makes an error and there's no corrective action, admission that a mistake was made or even a small apology. I recently discovered an error on my financial accounts and asked the bank how this was overlooked even after I had pointed out the error prior to the account being processed. Abby, I was completely ignored and never received any feedback. What's the best way to ask someone for an explanation concerning what actions were taken to ensure the error does not happen again? — <i>KEEN ON QUALITY</i></p><p><b>DEAR KEEN ON QUALITY:</b> In your line of work, safety was the top priority. You developed a zero-tolerance attitude toward errors because it was literally a matter of life and limb. Outside that environment, however, you may find it helpful to remember that the stakes are not nearly so high.</p><p>No permanent harm came of the bank error. You are right that it would be best if the bank reviewed its procedures to avoid future errors, but that's their job, not yours. Having corrected the error in a timely fashion, the bank owes you no further explanation. Trust that, in the future, they will do their best to improve without your help (but always check your statements).</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.summary: <p>The gruesome discovery of 56 decomposing bodies at South Chicago Chapel in South Deering has raised concerns about the regulation of Illinois funeral homes. How did such neglect happen? And what’s being done about it?</p><h3>What happened at South Chicago Chapel funeral home?</h3><p>In August, Illinois authorities <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" ><u>shut down</u></a> South Chicago Chapel in South Deering after receiving a tip that owners Clark and Johanna Morgan were improperly storing bodies. Inside the funeral home, investigators found dozens of bodies in various stages of decomposition.</p><p>After the investigation, the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation suspended Johanna Morgan’s funeral director and embalmer’s license, and the agency is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/09/21/south-chicago-chapel-johanna-clark-morgan-funeral-home-decomposing-bodies-revocation-hearing" ><u>seeking to revoke</u></a> it permanently.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/08/10/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-oversight-illinois-decomposing-bodies" >The department</a> found the funeral home, 2939 E. 95th St., was “a danger to the public safety, interest and welfare.” It alleged South Chicago Chapel let “multiple decedents to be kept in an unrefrigerated area with deplorable conditions, including rodent infestation, causing decomposition and maggot infestation of the bodies.”</p><h3>Have South Chicago Chapel’s owners been in trouble before?</h3><p>Yes. The August shutdown was the second time in two years authorities have responded to allegations of misconduct against <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/07/owners-of-far-south-side-funeral-home-have-history-of-mishandling-human-remains" ><u>Clark and Johanna Morgan</u></a>.</p><p>In early 2025, the state shut down Heights Crematory in Chicago Heights, also operated by the Morgans, for mishandling the remains of about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/06/19/chicago-heights-crematory-bodies-death-license-closed" ><u>100 people</u></a>.</p><p>That prompted a new state law expanding the regulatory authority of the Illinois comptroller’s office, which, in a quirk of state responsibilities, oversees crematories in addition to its fiscal duties.</p><p>There were other <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/09/01/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-bodies-clark-johanna-morgan" ><u>red flags</u></a> over the years involving the Morgans:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-3c7036d5-b75b-11f1-af38-bfba948b12b7"><li>Evergreen Park police found two bodies in the Morgans’ van on their residential block in 2024.<br></li><li>The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation suspended Clark Morgan’s funeral director and embalmer license in 2018 due to failure to file or pay state income taxes.<br></li><li>In April 2024, the agency fined Clark Morgan $10,000 and revoked his license due to “unprofessional conduct” and practicing on an expired license. <br></li></ul><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-3c705de0-b75b-11f1-af38-bfba948b12b7"><li>South Chicago Chapel had a history of failed building inspections. In addition, city building inspectors hadn’t done an annual inspection for the past four years. <br></li><li>Property tax bills were also delinquent for the past two years, and the Illinois Department of Revenue issued four liens on the Morgans’ home from 2022 to 2026.<br></li></ul><h3>What happened at Bohemian National Cemetery?</h3><p>In a separate case earlier this summer,<b> </b>investigators from the state comptroller’s office visited <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/09/bohemian-national-cemetery-under-investigation-for-improperly-stored-remains-equipment-failures" ><u>Bohemian National Cemetery</u></a><b> </b>in North Park after a July 21 tip. They found “multiple equipment failures and some human remains waiting to be cremated that were not maintained at the proper temperature,” according to a statement from the comptroller’s office.</p><p>By the end of July, the comptroller’s office had shut down Bohemian. The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation was “made aware” that South Chicago Chapel used the crematorium so “proactively conducted an on-site visit” to the funeral home, the agency said in a statement to the Sun-Times.</p><p>In the wake of recent investigations at Bohemian and Heights Crematory, Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza said she was “thankful” a new state law taking effect Jan. 1 will allow her office to “summarily suspend a crematory license without a prior hearing and immediately inspect the premises and records in egregious cases.”</p><div They went there to ask about the location of their mother’s remains. The two believe their mother’s remains are not in the urn, which contains a bag full of what they suspect are rocks, not ashes. The bag is labeled “Bohemian National Cemetery.” The two said they signed with Planet Green Cremations to handle their mother’s remains and do not know how South Chicago Chapel or Bohemian National Cemetery got involved in the process.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Who oversees Illinois’ funeral homes and crematories?</h3><p>The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation regulates funeral directors and embalmers. The department can conduct in-person inspections without receiving a tip, but it is a complaint-driven agency and does not conduct periodic inspections on all facilities, according to the department.</p><p>Apparently <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/08/10/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-oversight-illinois-decomposing-bodies" >no state agency oversees funeral homes themselves</a>, at their physical locations, officials said.</p><p>After the Chicago Heights Crematory case, Mendoza spearheaded <a class="Link" href="https://illinoiscomptroller.gov/newsroom/press-releases/comptroller-susana-mendozas-legislation-strengthening-the-offices-oversight-of-crematoriums-signed-into-law" target="_blank" ><u>legislation</u></a> that gives the comptroller's office more investigative authority over crematories.</p><p>The bill authorizes the comptroller’s office to suspend a crematory license immediately in extreme cases and immediately do inspections after receiving a complaint, and it raises penalties to $10,000 per violation. The bill was signed into law this summer and takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation and the Illinois comptroller’s office have the authority to suspend and revoke licenses, impose fines and take other disciplinary measures. But according to that department, it doesn't have authority to bring criminal charges. Any suspected criminal activity would be investigated by law enforcement and charges would be brought by a state’s attorney.</p><h3>Are changes coming to oversight of the death care industry?</h3><p>In light of what happened at South Chicago Chapel, some legislators are talking about reforms. State Rep. Diane Blair-Sherlock, D-Villa Park, who co-sponsored the 2025 crematory legislation, said the state should consider putting funeral homes, crematories and licensing under a single authority. No bill has been proposed yet.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker has questioned who should investigate funeral homes but has said little else about what kind of legislative response should follow.</p><h3>Have criminal charges been filed against South Chicago Chapel?</h3><p>Criminal charges haven’t been filed yet in spite of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/30/south-chicago-chapel-decomposing-bodies-funeral-home-vigil-families" >demands from families</a> and people affected.</p><p>Chicago police are still investigating what happened at South Chicago Chapel. In August, the Cook County medical examiner’s office was still working to identify all the deceased, as well as the cremated remains of at least 56 more people.</p><p>In August, comptroller spokesperson Kim Howard said the office “referred our findings and met with the Cook County state’s attorney’s office and [Illinois State Police] in hopes of criminal charges being filed.”</p><p>Illinois State Police are still investigating the Chicago Heights crematory situation and are also assisting Chicago Police on the South Chicago Chapel investigation.</p><h3>What lawsuits have been filed against South Chicago Chapel?</h3><p>The city of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/08/31/clark-johanna-morgan-south-chicago-chapel-decomposing-bodies-lawsuit-building-department" >Chicago is suing the owners</a> of South Chicago Chapel for a litany of alleged building code violations, including the failure to keep buildings “clean, sanitary, and safe.” The city is asking a judge to issue a fine of $11,500 per day for every day the violations are not corrected.</p><p>The Morgans have been summoned to the first hearing of the Buildings Department’s lawsuit on Sept. 24 in Cook County Circuit Court.</p><p>In addition, a Texas woman launched a potential <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/11/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-bodies-mishandled-class-action-lawsuit" ><u>class-action lawsuit</u></a> in August, alleging South Chicago Chapel mishandled the remains of her father along with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" target="_blank" ><u>dozens of other bodies</u></a>.</p><h3>Is the way Illinois regulates funeral homes unusual?</h3><p>Yes. Illinois is one of four states — along with Alaska, Hawaii and Iowa — that does not conduct any inspections of licensed funeral homes, crematories or cemeteries, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://theconferenceonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Regulations-in-Licensing-2025-Finalized.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>2025 survey</u></a> from the International Conference of Funeral Service Examining Boards.</p><p>A vast majority of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/18/south-deering-funeral-home-decomposing-bodies-illinois-lax-oversight-inspections" ><u>other states carry out annual or biannual inspections</u></a> of funeral homes and sometimes even unannounced visits.</p><p>Illinois also is the only state that does not have a board or agency monitoring licensed funeral homes at their physical locations.</p><p>Thirty-six states have separate funeral boards to manage director licenses, funeral homes, crematories and cemeteries. The other states, excluding Illinois, have appointed state agencies, such as public health departments, to the task.</p><h3>Does the city of Chicago regulate funeral homes?</h3><p>Not directly. If a funeral home sells products, such as caskets or flowers, they must obtain a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/07/owners-of-far-south-side-funeral-home-have-history-of-mishandling-human-remains" ><u>business license</u></a> issued by the Chicago Department of Business Affairs and Consumer Protection.</p><p>South Chicago Chapel does not have a Chicago business license, said a spokesperson for that department.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule entries.title: Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity Mirror Rooms return to Chicago this fall at Wrightwood 659
entries.summary: <p>On the second floor of Wrightwood 659, sits a portal to another world. Or, rather, two portals.</p><p>The boutique art museum in Lincoln Park is currently displaying two Infinity Mirror Rooms, the colorful, reflective and immersive artworks from the wildly popular Japanese artist <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/26/1102916697/yayoi-kusama-high-priestess-of-polka-dots-has-died" target="_blank" ><u>Yayoi Kusama</u></a>, who died in August at the age of 97.</p><p>The show at Wrightwood, “<a class="Link" href="https://wrightwood659.org/exhibitions/inner-worlds-visions-from-the-hirshhorn-collection/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24232358838&gbraid=0AAAAA9gf_bcO6dLEl_E7okwTCkd_IIrIY&gclid=Cj0KCQjw8c3VBhCsARIsAA_xJ92mjTrP4vNBtlLPmzYr_oHNQwDYfboVPaG0ahvKrWf-w6GXWgjgl6AaAkmvEALw_wcB" target="_blank" ><u>Inner Worlds: Visions from the Hirshhorn Collection</u></a>,” opens Friday and runs through Dec. 19. It is currently the only place in Chicago to experience Kusama’s mirrored rooms. Local audiences may be familiar with Kusama’s work from Chicago’s WNDR Museum, which, before it closed for good this month, featured the infinity room titled “<a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagogallerynews.com/articles/wndr-museum-announces-redesigned-yayoi-kusma-space-and-new-lounge-in-west-loop" target="_blank" ><u>LOVE IS CALLING</u></a>.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ac0000" name="module-ac0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Inner Worlds: Visions from the Hirshhorn Collection</h3><br><b>When:</b> Sept. 25-Dec. 19<br><b>Where:</b> Wrightwood 659, 659 W. Wrightwood Ave.<br><b>Tickets:</b> $20<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://wrightwood659.org/exhibitions/inner-worlds-visions-from-the-hirshhorn-collection/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24232358838&gbraid=0AAAAA9gf_bcO6dLEl_E7okwTCkd_IIrIY&gclid=Cj0KCQjw8c3VBhCsARIsAA_xJ92mjTrP4vNBtlLPmzYr_oHNQwDYfboVPaG0ahvKrWf-w6GXWgjgl6AaAkmvEALw_wcB" target="_blank" >wrightwood659.org</a></div> </div><p>While Kusama developed the Infinity Mirror Rooms for decades — in fact, the show at Wrightwood features her first from 1965 — they had a resurgence in widespread popularity beginning in 2017, when the exhibit, “Yayoi Kusama: Infinity Mirrors,” toured the country. The show drew <a class="Link" href="https://www.si.edu/newsdesk/releases/hirshhorn-s-yayoi-kusama-infinity-mirrors-breaks-records" target="_blank" ><u>record attendance levels</u></a> at several museums and generated tremendous internet buzz, with visitors posting their mirrored art selfies to Instagram.</p><p>The moment helped to solidify Kusama’s place not only in art history, but also in pop culture. It led to her personal appearance — a blunt red bob and colorful dresses with geometric patterns — becoming as instantly recognizable as the polka dots and pumpkins often featured in her work.</p><p>But those bright colored motifs were pulled from Kusama’s own internal struggles. Throughout her life, the avant-garde artist talked openly about experiencing hallucinations, which began when she was a young child and led her to art. She also lived voluntarily at a psychiatric facility in Tokyo from the 1970s until her death.</p><p>That 2017 exhibit was organized by the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, the Smithsonian’s modern and contemporary art museum, which also curated the show at Wrightwood.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jim Urquhart/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In the new show, three of Kusama’s iconic works — two mirrored rooms and one large pumpkin sculpture — are presented alongside two of her art peers, Mary Bauermeister and Niki de Saint Phalle. Each of the women was a trailblazing 20th-century artist who forged careers at a time when the art world was still overwhelmingly male-dominated.</p><p>Plus, each of the women explored their own inner worlds and thought about how to immerse audiences in their work, including Bauermeister’s optical boxes, two of which are featured in the show and require a viewer to peer through a lens to catch sight of the drawing beneath.</p><p>Shown together, it allows audiences to understand Kusama’s work in the context of what else was happening in the art world throughout the 1950s and ’60s, a period in which all three of the women lived in New York. And already the Chicago show is attracting attention; Wrightwood staff say it is the most preregistrations they have ever had for an exhibition.</p><p>“People know Kusama really well, but we said it would be really great to spread out and look at who else was doing this,” said curator Betsy Johnson, who works at the Hirshhorn. “Who have [people] maybe not heard of yet? Who can we put in Kusama's company? And it very quickly came to the fore that Niki de Saint-Phalle and Mary Bauermeister were just such a good fit.”</p><p>While Kusama reached certified superstar status in her later years of life, she was not without controversy. After her death in August, <a class="Link" href="https://www.hawaiipublicradio.org/local-news/2026-09-10/japanese-artist-yayoi-kusama-death-revives-history-of-racist-remarks" target="_blank" ><u>racist anti-Black comments</u></a> she wrote in her autobiography resurfaced. Vice’s Dexter Thomas pointed out <a class="Link" href="https://www.vice.com/en/article/japans-most-famous-avant-garde-artist-banned-us-from-her-studio/" target="_blank" ><u>in 2017</u></a> that that section was removed from the English-language translation of the text. Thomas, who is Black, also reported on being banned from Kusama’s studio.</p><p>Kusama issued an apology in 2023, saying in a statement to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.sfchronicle.com/entertainment/article/yayoi-kusama-sfmoma-apology-18424518.php" target="_blank" ><u>San Francisco Chronicle</u></a>, “I deeply regret using hurtful and offensive language in my book. My message has always been one of love, hope, compassion, and respect for all people. My lifelong intention has been to lift up humanity through my art. I apologize for the pain I have caused.”</p><p>Johnson, who pointed both to Kusama’s ongoing mental illness and upbringing in a homogeneous culture, said the new Wrightwood exhibit does not directly address Kusama’s past comments.</p><p>“We definitely come upon these very unique individuals who may have mental illness, as Kusama did, and so their interactions with society are maybe not always along the same lines as one would hope,” Johnson said. “I think, in addition to her mental illness, there were probably also cultural conditions that were probably more challenging for her, but I do know that she did apologize, later in life, for making racist comments.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Option attack lifts improving St. Ignatius into Super 25 rankings
entries.summary: <p>As more teams in the Catholic League shift toward spread offenses, St. Ignatius has stayed true to its triple-option attack under coach Matt Miller.</p><p>The Wolfpack missed the IHSA playoffs each of the last two years, but Miller and his program slowly built momentum back with a pair of Prep Bowl championships. Those championships set the table for a resurgent 2026 season. Behind players like Nino Capuano and Reid Hites, St. Ignatius has improved more than arguably any Catholic League team.</p><p>“We knew that we were very talented and we could go really far,” Capuano, a sophomore, said. “If you’re looking from an outside perspective as a fan or other teams, I feel like a lot of people doubted us thinking we were going to be the same Ignatius from the past two years.</p><p>Playoff-bound for the first time since 2023, St. Ignatius (4-1, 1-0 CCL Orange) has already doubled its regular-season win total from a year ago. The Wolfpack have beaten quality opponents too, defeating defending Class 6A champion Fenwick and Class 7A finalist St. Rita. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/09/20/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >St. Ignatius joined the Super 25 rankings on Sunday.</a></p><p>St. Ignatius is averaging 39.2 points per game through five weeks, nearly twice its scoring number from last season.</p><p>“We’re in a position that I thought we would be,” Miller said. “We expected to be in this spot competing for a division title, so I wouldn’t say it’s a surprise. That’s been the goal of our players. We want to win a state championship regardless of what class we’re in.”</p><p>Capuano set a new school record for rushing yards against St. Rita. The 5-7, 180-pounder erupted for 279 yards and three scores in a 42-16 victory.</p><p>“My field vision has gotten a lot better,” Capuano said. “I went to a lot of camps to get better at my position. I’ve made a huge all-around jump in running the ball.”</p><p>Hites, meanwhile, has captained the St. Ignatius offense since he returned from elbow surgery late in his sophomore year. The junior quarterback accounted for six touchdowns in only 8.5 quarters of work over the team’s first three games this year.</p><p>Hites’ older brother Connor is a key factor on the Wolfpack defense at safety. He intercepted two passes, made two sacks and totaled 10 tackles against Hope Academy. He then helped contain Iowa recruit Jake Thies in the 30-20 win over Fenwick, recording 12 tackles, one sack and one forced fumble.</p><p>St. Ignatius’ only loss came against unbeaten IC Catholic and the Wolfpack has allowed just 64 points in five games. The win over Fenwick was St. Ignatius’s first divisional victory since 2023, when the Wolfpack won the Green with a 3-0 mark.</p><p>“Our connection this year is a lot stronger than it’s been in years past,” Reid Hites said. “Our goals are a lot bigger and I feel like we had a different mentality going into the season. We don’t want to be overlooked anymore and I feel like our work has paid off so far...With the Fenwick game and the Rita game, we went into those games overlooked, but from within, everyone on the team knew we could win those games. That was the ultimate goal and we did that.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.shawlocal.com/friday-night-drive/" target="_blank" >Read more high school football coverage at Friday Night Drive.</a></p>

entries.title: Dual-threat quarterback Will Clark has kept Fremd on the winning track
entries.summary: <p>Will Clark had a hard act to follow at Fremd.</p><p>Last year as a sophomore, Clark was the backup to Vikings quarterback Johnny O'Brien. Now at Northwestern, O'Brien was a three-year starter who piled up 8.395 total yards and 93 touchdowns in his prep career.</p><p>No surprise, O'Brien got virtually all the practice reps. But when he missed a Week 7 game at Barrington with an injury, Clark was pressed into action for his first varsity start.</p><p>Barrington won 23-7 and Clark was 9 of 19 passing for 156 yards. But he learned some valuable lessons that are paying off this season.</p><p>With Clark as the starter this year, Fremd is 4-1. Through the first five games of the season, Clark had thrown for 1,081 yards with three TDs.</p><p>"Ever since that [Barrington loss], I've had ... this chip on my shoulder to do a lot better," Clark told the Sun-Times. "And I'd say that my preparation is a lot different now for each game. I feel like last year, sometimes I got off track. But this year I've been very focused and learning a lot of things from the coaches."</p><p>He also picked up plenty from watching O'Brien on and off the field.</p><p>"I learned a lot from him," Clark said. "Like ... you have to watch your film. You have to know what the defense is doing at all times. And then in actual game situations — reading the defense and your footwork and everything, I learned a lot from that."</p><p>O'Brien is 6-3 and 200 pounds, 3 inches taller and 30 pounds heavier than Clark, so it's no surprise they have different profiles.</p><p>Clark is being used as more of a dual-threat quarterback than O'Brien.</p><p>"He's had some longer runs," Fremd coach Lou Sponsel said of Clark. "He's had some designed runs. Like Week 1, [Lake Zurich was] overshifting to take away some of our stuff in the pass game so we let Will run our zone game into the boundaries.</p><p>"And Johnny could have run, too. We just said, no, we're not running Johnny."</p><p>Meanwhile, Sponsel said Clark is developing as a pocket passer. "But he's still got that dual threat to where he can scramble. He can run at any time, either as a designed quarterback run or he just takes off and runs," Sponsel said.</p><p>Clark is comfortable in either phase of the game.</p><p>"I've always liked to use my feet whenever I get the chance to," he said. "And I also love chucking the ball down the field and making plays doing that."</p><p>Even if he wasn't following in the footsteps of a Power Four recruit, Clark knew he'd be in the spotlight as the starting quarterback for a high-profile program. Win or lose, taking heat or praise, he lets it roll off his back.</p><p>"I always stay away from that," he said of the outside noise. "I don't pay attention to that at all. I always move on from it, next play mentality, next game mentality."</p><p>Similarly, during the school year and the summer, Clark toggles back and forth between two sports: football and baseball. He also played basketball, but gave it up after eighth grade.</p><p>"When it comes to baseball and football, sometimes when I need a break from one of them I always just go to the next," he said.</p><p>For now, though, he's enjoying this football ride.</p>

entries.title: Man, 18, accused of fatally stabbing woman, 18, in Englewood
entries.summary: <p>An 18-year-old man is accused of fatally stabbing an 18-year-old woman to death early Tuesday in Englewood.</p><p>Alfredo Tzoy, 18, was charged with murder and was scheduled to appear for a detention hearing Thursday.</p><p>Tzoy, of the Englewood neighborhood, was arrested shortly after the attack, which left the still-unidentified 18-year-old woman dead, police and the Cook County medical examiner’s office said.</p><p>She was found on the ground in the 7300 block of South Emerald Avenue, with a stab wound to the neck. She was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where she was pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>Officers searching the area discovered Tzoy on a nearby porch with a cut to his right hand, police said.</p><p>A knife was recovered. </p>
